Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 41
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Fast Food Worker
  trauma_type: Witnessed other trauma
  pcl5: 64

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Being Criticised: Being criticised or corrected, Time of Day: The same time of day the event occurred, Auditory (Loud Noises): Loud noises
  Threat: Safe Zone Only: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places, Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening, Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds

Vignette:
Amir is a 41-year-old fast food worker, single and living alone in a small apartment near the restaurant where he has worked for the past seven years. The event that changed everything happened fifteen months ago, on a Tuesday evening during the closing shift. A customer who had been waiting in line for several minutes suddenly began shouting at the cashier, a young woman named Leila. Amir was at the fry station, and he remembers the sound of the argument escalating—the customer’s voice rising, the manager’s attempt to intervene. Then he heard a loud crack, a sound he later learned was a gunshot. He saw Leila fall; he saw the customer drop the weapon and flee. Amir did nothing—he stood frozen behind the counter, his hands still gripping a metal basket, his ears ringing. He did not run, did not call for help until someone else did. In the months that followed, that moment replayed in his mind not as a coherent story but as a jumble of sensations: the heat of the fry oil, the ringing silence after the shot, the way Leila’s eyes went wide. He had come to believe that his immobility meant he was cowardly, that he had failed her. He was certain that if he had stepped forward, he might have prevented it, even though he knew, logically, that he was unarmed.

The first trigger he noticed was the time of day. The incident happened at 9:15 PM, during the last hour before the restaurant closed. Now, every evening as the clock nears nine, Amir feels a physical tightening in his chest. He has changed his schedule to work only morning and early afternoon shifts, so that he can leave before that hour arrives. His manager has complained, but Amir has offered no real explanation. Being at the restaurant at all is difficult, but the morning is bearable. The real trouble began with being criticised or corrected. When a customer complains about his order, or when the shift supervisor tells him he is moving too slowly, Amir’s heart hammers and he feels a wave of dread—as though the criticism is a prelude to something worse. He has been told he overreacts to simple feedback; once, when a manager asked him to re-clean a counter, Amir walked off the floor and locked himself in the supply closet for ten minutes. He knew it made no sense, but in that moment he was certain that being singled out would lead to another violent confrontation. Similarly, when something takes longer than expected—a delivery truck that is late, a customer who cannot decide on an order—he finds himself scanning the room for exits, assuming that a delay means danger is approaching. He monitors every unexpected sound: the slam of a refrigerator door, the hiss of a pressure fryer, a dropped tray. He is on high alert for any loud noise, and his startle response has become so intense that coworkers now avoid surprising him. He has lost count of how many times he has dropped a tray himself because a sudden bang made him flinch.

The only places Amir feels safe are his apartment and, oddly, the restaurant’s walk-in cooler—a small, windowless room where the hum of compressors drowns out other sounds. He has started taking his breaks there, sitting on a crate of lettuce. His occupational life has narrowed: he no longer works the register, avoids the front counter, and will not go near the spot where Leila fell. His supervisor has written him up twice for unprofessional behaviour, and a third incident would likely lead to termination. Amir knows he is close to losing his job, but the idea of finding another position feels impossible if the same fears follow him.

He finally sought help after a night when a car backfired outside his building and he spent three hours huddled in his bathroom, certain that someone was coming for him. What he fears most is that he will never feel normal again—that he is stuck inside a mind that turns every ordinary moment into a threat. What he hopes for, though he can barely say it aloud, is that talking about what he saw might loosen its grip, that he might one day walk through the restaurant without feeling the ghost of that gunshot in his ears.
